methodological_rigor.justification: This is a single-center retrospective cohort of 175 locally advanced rectal cancer patients treated with nCRT and laparoscopic surgery, comparing outcomes by a dichotomized interval (<=6 vs >6 weeks) (Methods; Results). Eligibility criteria and treatment regimen are described, and follow-up is long (median 71 months), but treatment timing is not randomized and could reflect scheduling/clinical factors not captured in the dataset (Methods; Discussion limitations). The analyses (KM/log-rank, ROC for interval as a predictor, and Cox regression with multivariable adjustment) are appropriate, though power for detecting interval effects appears limited and the median-split interval may dilute nonlinear relationships (Results; Discussion).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is an individual retrospective cohort study, consistent with Oxford LoE 2b (Methods). The question is clinically relevant because nCRT-to-surgery timing is a common management decision in LARC and may influence pCR, complications, and survival (Introduction). In this cohort, interval category was not associated with pCR, OS, or RFS, suggesting limited actionable impact beyond reassurance that waiting beyond 6 weeks was not worse within this setting (Results; Conclusions).

reporting_quality.justification: An observational reporting standard (STROBE) is appropriate, and the manuscript reports setting, inclusion/exclusion criteria, treatment details, endpoints (OS/RFS/pCR/complications), and core statistical methods (Methods; Results). Key numerical results are provided for group comparisons and multivariable hazard ratios for ypStage and procedure type (Results). The normalized manuscript does not describe public sharing of the dataset or analysis code, limiting reproducibility beyond the described methods (Data/code availability not stated).

novelty_literature.justification: The study addresses a well-studied clinical question (optimal nCRT-to-surgery interval) with an additional long-term single-center cohort contribution rather than a new concept or method (Introduction; Discussion). The main finding is a null association between a 6-week threshold and OS/RFS/pCR, which is consistent with mixed prior literature rather than field-shifting (Results; Discussion). Novelty is therefore incremental and context-specific.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract and results clearly define the interval groups, endpoints (OS/RFS/pCR/complications), and the principal null findings with supporting p-values and HRs (Abstract; Results). Methods are organized with concrete definitions for inclusion, nCRT regimen, and statistical plan (Methods). The discussion situates findings against prior trials and meta-analyses and explicitly acknowledges retrospective design and limited power (Discussion).

key_strengths: Long-term follow-up (median 71 months) in a defined LARC cohort with standardized nCRT regimen and laparoscopic surgery approach.
Appropriate survival analyses (KM/log-rank and multivariable Cox) and explicit reporting that ypStage III strongly predicts OS/RFS compared with pCR.
Pragmatic clinical message that, in this cohort, delaying surgery beyond 6 weeks did not worsen pCR, OS, RFS, or complications.
key_concerns: Retrospective, single-center design with non-randomized timing introduces potential selection and confounding that may not be captured by covariates in the Cox model.
Interval exposure definition is a median split (<=6 vs >6 weeks) which may miss clinically important nonlinear thresholds (eg 8-12 weeks) and reduces sensitivity.
Power appears limited for detecting modest interval effects, and follow-up differed between groups (Results), raising risk of residual bias.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a competent retrospective cohort study with a clear null result and useful prognostic modeling, but limitations in design, exposure definition, and power make it better suited to a tier-3 venue after revisions that strengthen confounding discussion and sensitivity analyses.
